mn54:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the country of the Anguttarāpans. There is a town of theirs called Āpaṇa.
mn54:2.1: Now when it was morning, the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he went into Āpaṇa for alms.
mn54:2.2: When he had wandered for alms in Āpaṇa and returned from his alms-round after his meal, he went to a certain grove for the day’s abiding,
mn54:2.3: and he went into the grove and sat down at the root of a tree for the day’s abiding.
mn54:3.1: Potaliya the householder, wearing full dress with parasol and sandals also went to the grove, walking and wandering for exercise, and when he had gone into the grove he went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him,
mn54:3.2: and when the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he stood at one side. When he had done so, the Blessed One said to him:
mn54:3.3: ‘There are seats, householder, sit down if you like.’
mn54:3.4: When this was said, the householder Potaliya (thought): ‘The monk Gotama addresses me with the word “householder”,’ and he was annoyed and displeased and remained silent.
mn54:3.6: and a third time the Blessed One said to him:
mn54:3.7: ‘There are seats, householder, sit down if you like.’
mn54:3.8: When this was said, the householder Potaliya (thought): ‘The monk Gotama addresses me with the word “householder”,’ and he was annoyed and displeased, and he said:
mn54:3.9: ‘Master Gotama, it is neither fitting nor proper that you address me with the word “householder”.’
mn54:3.10: ‘Householder, you have the aspects, marks and signs of a householder.’
mn54:3.11: ‘Nevertheless, Master Gotama, I have given up all my works and am cut off from all my affairs.’
mn54:3.12: ‘In what way have you given up all your works, householder, and are cut off from all your affairs?’
mn54:3.13: ‘Master Gotama, whatever property or corn, silver or gold I had I have consigned it all as an inheritance to my children. I live on that, without giving advice or reproof, using just enough for food and clothing.
mn54:3.14: That is how I have given up all my works and am cut off from all my affairs.’
mn54:3.15: ‘Householder, being cut off from affairs as you describe it is one and being cut off from affairs in the Noble Ones’ Discipline is another.’
mn54:3.16: ‘How is being cut off from affairs in the Noble Ones’ Discipline, then, venerable sir?
mn54:3.17: It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma showing how being cut off from affairs is in the Noble Ones’ Discipline.’
mn54:3.18: ‘Then listen, householder, and heed well what I shall say.’
mn54:4.2: ‘Householder, there are eight dhammas in the Noble Ones’ Discipline that lead to the cutting off of affairs.
mn54:4.4: Killing of living beings is to be abandoned with the support of non-killing of living beings;
mn54:4.5: Taking of what is not given is to be abandoned with the support of taking what is given.
mn54:4.6: False speech is to be abandoned with the support of true speech.
mn54:4.7: Malicious speech is to be abandoned with the support of unmalicious speech.
mn54:4.8: Rapacious greed is to be abandoned with the support of absence of rapacious greed.
mn54:4.9: Spiteful revenge is to be abandoned with the support of absence of spiteful revenge.
mn54:4.10: Angry despair is to be abandoned with the support of absence of angry despair.
mn54:4.11: Pride is to be abandoned with the support of non-pride.
mn54:4.12: These are the eight dhammas, stated in brief without expounding the details, that lead in the Noble Ones’ Discipline to the cutting off of affairs.’
mn54:5.1: ‘Venerable sir, it would be good if, out of pity, the Blessed One expounds the details of these eight dhammas that lead in the Noble Ones’ Discipline to the cutting off of affairs, which have been stated in brief by the Blessed One without expounding the details.’
mn54:5.2: ‘Then listen, householder, and heed well what I shall say.’
mn54:6.1: ‘”Killing living beings is to be abandoned with the support of non-killing of living beings”, so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?
mn54:6.2: Here a noble disciple considers thus:
mn54:6.3: “I am practising the way to the abandoning, the cutting off, of those fetters which are the reason for my killing living beings.
mn54:6.4: Were I to be a killer of living beings, (my) self would blame me for that, the wise would judge and censure me for that and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination is to be expected owing to that.
mn54:6.5: But this killing of living beings is itself a fetter and a hindrance.
mn54:6.6: And while taints and fever of defilement might arise owing to the killing of living beings, there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who abstains from killing living beings.”
mn54:6.7: “Killing of living beings is to be abandoned with the support of non-killing of living beings.”
mn54:6.8: So it is with reference to this that it was said.
mn54:7.1: “‘Taking what is not given is to be abandoned with the support of taking what is given”; so it was said …
mn54:7.3: “I am practising the way to the abandoning, the cutting off, of those fetters which are the reason for my taking what is not given …
mn54:7.4: (my) self would blame me for that, the wise would judge and censure me for that, and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination is to be expected owing to that …
mn54:7.6: there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who abstains from taking what is not given” …
mn54:8.1: “‘False speech is to be abandoned with the support of true speech”; so it was said …
mn54:8.3: “I am practising the way to the abandoning, the cutting off, of those fetters which are the reason for my speaking falsehood …
mn54:8.4: (my) self would blame me for that, the wise would judge and censure me for that, and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination is to be expected owing to that
mn54:8.6: there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who abstains from false speech”
mn54:9.1: “‘Malicious speech is to be abandoned with the support of unmalicious speech”; so it was said …
mn54:9.3: “I am practising the way to the abandoning, the cutting off, of those fetters which are the reason for my speaking maliciously …
mn54:9.4: (my) self would blame me for that, the wise would judge and censure me for that, and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination is to be expected owing to that
mn54:9.6: there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who abstains from malicious speech”
mn54:10.1: “‘Rapacious greed is to be abandoned with the support of absence of rapacious greed”; so it was said …
mn54:10.3: “I am practising the way to the abandoning, the cutting off, of those fetters which are the reason for my being rapaciously greedy …
mn54:10.4: (my) self would blame me for that, the wise would judge and censure me for that, and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination is to be expected owing to that
mn54:10.6: there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who is not rapaciously greedy”
mn54:11.1: ‘ “Spiteful revenge is to be abandoned with the support of absence of spiteful revenge”; so it was said ...
mn54:11.3: “I am practising the way to the abandoning, the cutting off, of those fetters which are the reason for my being spitefully revengeful …
mn54:11.4: (my) self would blame me for that, the wise would judge and censure me for that, and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination is to be expected owing to that
mn54:11.6: there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who is not spitefully revengeful”
mn54:12.1: ‘ “Angry despair is to be abandoned with the support of absence of angry despair”; so it was said …
mn54:12.3: “I am practising the way to the abandoning, the cutting off, of those fetters which are the reason for my angry despairing …
mn54:12.4: (my) self would blame me for that, the wise would judge and censure me for that, and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination is to be expected owing to that …
mn54:12.6: there are no taints or fever of defilement in one who is not angrily despair.”
mn54:12.7: So it was with reference to this that it was said: “Angry despair is to be abandoned with the support of absence of angry despair.” ’
mn54:13.1: ‘ “Pride is to be abandoned with the support of non-pride”; so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?
mn54:13.2: Here a noble disciple considers thus:
mn54:13.3: “I am practising the way to the abandoning, the cutting off, of those fetters which are the reason for my being proud.
mn54:13.4: Were I to be proud, (my) self would blame me for that, the wise would judge and censure me for that, and on the dissolution of the body, after death, an unhappy destination is to be expected owing to that.
mn54:13.5: But this pride is itself a fetter and a hindrance.
mn54:13.6: And while taints and fever defilement might arise owing to pride, there are no taints and fever of defilement in one who is not proud.”
mn54:13.7: “Pride is to be abandoned with the support of non-pride.” ’
mn54:13.8: So it was for this reason that it was said,
mn54:14.1: ‘These eight dhammas, stated in brief, which lead in the Noble One’s Discipline to the cutting off of affairs, have now been expounded in detail.
mn54:14.2: But the cutting off of affairs in the Noble Ones’ Discipline has not yet been achieved altogether and in all ways.’
mn54:14.3: ‘Venerable sir, how does the cutting off of affairs come to pass in the Noble Ones’ Discipline altogether and in all ways?
mn54:14.4: It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would tell me that.’
mn54:14.5: ‘Then listen, householder and heed well what I shall say.’
mn54:15.1: ‘Householder, suppose a dog was waiting hungry and weak in a butcher’s shambles,
mn54:15.2: and then a skilled butcher or his apprentice carved out a skeleton of bones, blood-smeared but with no meat and he tossed it to the dog.
mn54:15.3: How do you conceive this, householder?
mn54:15.4: Would that dog get rid of his hunger and weakness by gnawing such a bone?’
mn54:15.7: ‘That skeleton of bones was well carved out, blood-smeared, with no meat;
mn54:15.8: eventually that dog would reap weariness and disappointment.’
mn54:15.9: ‘So too, householder, a noble disciple considers thus:
mn54:15.10: “Sensual desires have been compared to a skeleton of bones by the Blessed One as providing little enjoyment and much suffering and despair, while the danger in them is great,”
mn54:15.11: and having seen them thus as they actually are with right understanding, he eschews any kind of equanimity based on difference, supported by difference and develops only that kind of equanimity based on unity, supported by unity, where clinging to material things of the world ceases altogether without remainder.
mn54:16.1: ‘Householder, suppose a vulture, a crow or a kite seized a piece of meat and flew away,
mn54:16.2: and then vultures and crows and kites flew up and pecked and clawed it.
mn54:16.3: How do you conceive this, householder?
mn54:16.4: If that vulture, crow or kite did not soon relinquish that piece of meat, would he because of that incur death or deadly suffering?’
mn54:16.6: ‘So too, householder, a noble disciple considers thus:
mn54:16.7: “Sensual desires have been compared to a piece of meat by the Blessed One as providing little enjoyment and much suffering and despair, while the danger in them is great,”
mn54:16.8: and having seen them thus as they actually are with right understanding … clinging to material things of the world ceases altogether without remainder.
mn54:17.1: ‘Householder, suppose a man took a lighted grass torch and went against the wind.
mn54:17.2: How do you conceive this, householder?
mn54:17.3: If that man did not soon relinquish that lighted grass torch, would that lighted grass torch burn his hand or his arm or one or other of his limbs, and might he because of that incur death or deadly suffering?’
mn54:17.5: ‘So too, householder, a noble disciple considers thus:
mn54:17.6: “Sensual desires have been compared to a grass torch by the Blessed One as providing little enjoyment and much suffering and despair, while the danger in them is great,”
mn54:17.7: and having seen them thus as they actually are with right understanding … clinging to material things of the world ceases altogether without remainder.
mn54:18.1: ‘Householder, suppose there were a charcoal pit deeper than a man’s height full of glowing coals without flame or smoke,
mn54:18.2: and then a man came who wanted to live and not to die, who wanted pleasure and recoiled from pain,
mn54:18.3: and two strong men seized him by both arms and dragged him towards that charcoal pit.
mn54:18.4: How do you conceive this, householder?
mn54:18.5: Would that man fling his body this way and that?’
mn54:18.8: Because that man knows that if he falls into that charcoal pit, he will because of that incur death or deadly suffering.’
mn54:18.9: ‘So too, householder, a noble disciple considers thus:
mn54:18.10: “Sensual desires have been compared to a charcoal pit by the Blessed One as providing little enjoyment and much suffering and despair, while the danger in them is great”
mn54:18.11: and having seen them thus as they actually are with right understanding, he eschews any kind of equanimity based on difference, supported by difference and develops only that kind of equanimity based on unity, supported by unity, where clinging to material things of the world ceases altogether without remainder.
mn54:19.1: ‘Householder, suppose a man saw a dream with delightful parks, delightful groves, delightful meadows, delightful lakes
mn54:19.2: and on waking he saw nothing (of it),
mn54:19.3: so too a noble disciple considers thus:
mn54:19.4: “Sensual desires have been compared to a dream by the Blessed One as providing little enjoyment and much suffering and despair, while the danger in them is great”,
mn54:19.5: and having seen them thus as they actually are with right understanding … clinging to material things of the world ceases altogether without remainder.
mn54:20.1: ‘Householder, suppose a man borrowed property on loan: a smart carriage, or fine-jewelled earrings,
mn54:20.2: and preceded and surrounded by that borrowed property he went into the marketplace,
mn54:20.3: and then when people saw him, they spoke thus:
mn54:20.4: “Sirs, that is a rich man! That is how the rich enjoy their riches!”
mn54:20.5: and then the owners, whenever they saw him, took back what was theirs.
mn54:20.6: How do you conceive this, householder? Would that be enough for that man to change (his mind)?’
mn54:20.9: Because the owners take back what is theirs.’
mn54:20.10: ‘So too, householder, a noble disciple considers thus:
mn54:20.11: “Sensual desires have been compared to a loan by the Blessed One as providing little enjoyment and much suffering and despair, while the danger in them is great”,
mn54:20.12: and having seen them thus as they actually are with right understanding … clinging to material things of the world ceases altogether without remainder.
mn54:21.1: ‘Householder, suppose there were a dense grove not far from some village or town
mn54:21.2: where there was a tree all in blossom but none of its flowers had fallen to the ground,
mn54:21.3: and then a man came needing flowers, seeking flowers, wandering in search of flowers
mn54:21.4: and he went into the tree all in blossom,
mn54:21.6: “This tree is all in blossom but none of its flowers have fallen to the ground;
mn54:21.7: still I know how to climb a tree,
mn54:21.8: so why should I not climb this tree and pick as many as I want and fill my pocket?”
mn54:21.10: and then a second man needing flowers, seeking flowers, wandering in search of flowers, taking a sharp axe, he too went into the grove
mn54:21.11: and saw that tree all in blossom,
mn54:21.13: “This tree is all in blossom, but none of its flowers have fallen to the ground;
mn54:21.14: but I do not know how to climb a tree,
mn54:21.15: so why should I not set about cutting this tree down at its root and pick as many as I want and fill my pocket?”
mn54:21.17: How do you conceive this, householder?
mn54:21.18: If that first man who has climbed the tree did not soon come down, might he break his hand when the tree fell, or his foot or one or other of his limbs, whereby he might incur death or deadly suffering?’
mn54:21.20: ‘So too, householder, a noble disciple considers thus:
mn54:21.21: “Sensual desires have been compared to a tree by the Blessed One as providing little enjoyment and much suffering and despair, while the danger in them is great”,
mn54:21.22: and having seen them thus as they actually are with right understanding, he eschews any kind of equanimity based on difference, supported by difference and develops only that kind of equanimity based on unity, supported by unity, where clinging to material things of the world ceases altogether without remainder.
mn54:22.1: ‘Having arrived at that same supreme mindfulness, the purity of which is due to equanimity (characteristic of the fourth jhāna), this noble disciple recollects his manifold past life
mn54:22.2: that is to say, one birth, two births ... five births, ten births … fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of (world) contraction, many aeons of (world) expansion, many aeons of [(world) contraction and expansion: There I was so named, of such a race, with such (qualities of) appearance, such was my nutriment, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-term; and passing away from there, I appeared elsewhere; and there too I was so named, of such a race, with such (qualities of) appearance, such was my nutriment, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-term; and passing away from there I appeared here. Thus with its details and particulars he recollects his manifold past life.
mn54:23.1: ‘Having arrived at that same supreme mindfulness, the purity of which is due to equanimity, with the heavenly eyesight, which is purified and surpasses the human, this noble disciple sees beings passing away and reappearing inferior and superior, fair and ugly, well-behaved and ill-behaved; I understood how beings pass on according to their kammas, thus: “These worthy beings who are ill-conducted in body, speech and mind, revilers of Noble Ones, wrong in their views, giving effect to wrong view in their kammas (actions), have on the dissolution of the body, after death, appeared in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination in perdition, even in hell; but these worthy beings, who are well-conducted in body, speech and mind, not revilers of Noble Ones, right in their views, giving effect to right view in their kammas (actions), have, on the dissolution of the body, after death, appeared in a good destination, even in the heavenly world”, thus with heavenly eyesight which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, well-behaved and ill-behaved; He understands how beings pass on according to their kamma.
mn54:24.1: ‘Having arrived at that same supreme mindfulness, the purity of which is due to equanimity, by realization himself with direct knowledge, this noble disciple here and now enters upon and abides in deliverance of the heart and deliverance by understanding that are taint-free with exhaustion of taints.
mn54:25.1: ‘At this point, householder, the cutting off of affairs in the Noble Ones’ Discipline has been achieved altogether and in all ways.
mn54:25.2: How do you conceive this, householder,
mn54:25.3: do you see in yourself any such cutting off of affairs as this cutting off of affairs in the Noble Ones’ Discipline when it is achieved altogether and in all ways?’
mn54:25.4: ‘Venerable sir, who am I that I should possess any such cutting off of affairs altogether and in all ways as it is in the Noble Ones’ Discipline?
mn54:25.5: I am far indeed from that, venerable sir.
mn54:25.6: For, venerable sir, while the Wanderers of other sects do not know, we conceived that they knew; while they do not know, we fed them as one feeds those who know; while they do not know, we set them in the place of those who know.
mn54:25.7: But while the Bhikkhus know, we conceived that they did not know; while they know, we fed them as one feeds those who do not know; while they know, we set them in the place of those who do not know.
mn54:25.8: But now, venerable sir, while the Wanderers of other sects do not know, we shall know that they do not know; while they do not know, we shall feed them as one feeds those who do not know; while they do not know, we shall set them in the place of those who do not know.
mn54:25.9: But while the Bhikkhus know, we shall know that they know; while they know, we shall feed them as one feeds those that know; while they know, we shall set them in the place of those who know.
mn54:25.10: Venerable sir, the Blessed One knows my love for monks, my confidence in monks, my respect for monks.
mn54:26.2: The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama as though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, holding up a lamp in the darkness for those with eyesight to see forms.
mn54:26.3: ‘I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma and to the Sangha.
mn54:26.4: From today let Master, Gotama remember me as one who has gone to him for refuge for life.’
